phases.title: Pending Approvals 3 Plus Unregistered Ar Iter 1559
phases.desired_end_state: Auto-proposed from orphan task `pending-approvals-3-plus-unregistered-ar-iter-1559`. Last activity 2026-06-12T05:09:20.161842+00:00. Accept to claim the task_id into a drafting mission; dismiss to stop re-proposing.

draft.end_state: When this phase is done, one of two things is true: either this work item has been confirmed as real, given a concrete and agreed destination, and that destination has been delivered; or it has been judged not worth doing and retired so it stops resurfacing. As written, the facts do not yet define a concrete deliverable — the title points at something about pending approvals and unregistered approval requests, but what 'done' actually looks like is still an open question this brainstorm must pin down before anything else.
draft.why_now: This phase exists because a stale, unclaimed work item keeps being re-proposed and someone has to decide its fate. It traces back to activity that stopped around mid-June with nothing closed out, so it sits in limbo: not actively worked, not retired. The forcing function is the re-proposal itself — until it is either claimed and scoped or explicitly dismissed, it will keep demanding attention. Whether the underlying approvals/unregistered-request concern is still live is itself unverified and is part of what must be checked now.
draft.scope: IN: deciding whether this item is real and current; if real, nailing down a concrete destination and delivering it; if not, retiring it cleanly so it stops re-proposing. OUT: committing to any specific feature, fix, or behavior change before the underlying need is confirmed — the title alone is not enough to scope build work. Also OUT (pending confirmation) is broad rework of the approvals flow; this should stay narrowly aimed at whatever this single item actually represents, not become a general approvals overhaul.
draft.constraints_reuse: This should be assembly, not greenfield: if the item turns out to be real, prefer reusing the existing approvals and request-handling machinery already in place rather than building parallel paths. The hard constraint is that the live approvals flow must not break or regress while this is investigated or changed — anything touching it needs to leave the working path intact. Because the concrete subject is not yet confirmed, the specific components to reuse are an open question to resolve once scope is pinned.
draft.options_decision: The first real fork is dismiss versus claim. Dismissing costs nothing to build and stops the noise, but risks discarding a genuine gap if the concern is still live — cheap, but potentially a silent miss. Claiming lets the need be properly scoped and addressed, but spends effort on something whose value is unproven and may turn out stale. If claimed, a second fork follows: do a tightly-scoped investigation first to confirm the need before any build, versus going straight to a fix. Investigate-first is slower but avoids building against a phantom requirement. Recommendation: claim, but gate it on a short investigation that confirms the need is real and current before committing to any build; if the investigation finds nothing live, dismiss and retire it.
draft.risks_guardrails: Risk: building against an imagined requirement because the title was over-interpreted — guardrail: confirm the actual need from real signals before writing code, and keep a written 'what is this' answer before scoping. Risk: regressing the working approvals path while poking at it — guardrail: treat the live flow as not-to-break and verify it still works before and after any change. Risk: the item is simply stale and effort is wasted — guardrail: time-box the investigation and dismiss fast if nothing current surfaces. Risk: it gets dismissed but quietly resurfaces — guardrail: make dismissal explicit and durable so it actually stops re-proposing.
draft.done_gate: Done is checkable as: a recorded decision of either 'real, scoped, delivered' or 'retired, will not re-propose,' with no ambiguous middle. If retired: confirm it no longer re-proposes. If delivered: the agreed destination is met, the existing approvals path is verified still working (no regression), and whatever change was made is covered by a test that would catch the specific behavior it introduced or fixed. Because the deliverable is not yet defined, the precise pass/fail tests are an open item to fill in once scope is set in the steps below.
draft.breakdown: Step 1: triage — read the original signal behind this item and write a plain-language answer to 'what is this and is it still live,' deciding real vs. stale. Step 2: if stale, retire it durably and confirm it stops re-proposing — phase ends here. Step 3: if real, define the concrete destination and the specific in/out scope, replacing the placeholders above. Step 4: identify which existing approvals/request components to reuse and the exact path that must not break. Step 5: make the narrowest change that meets the destination. Step 6: add the test that proves the new behavior and re-verify the live flow is intact. Step 7: record the closeout so this does not resurface.

decisions: Claim this work item and investigate it, or dismiss it now and stop the re-proposals?
If claimed, do we require a short confirm-the-need investigation before any build, or accept going straight to a fix?
How much effort are you willing to spend confirming this is real before we cut our losses and retire it?
If it turns out real, should this stay a narrow point fix, or are you open to it touching the broader approvals flow?

projects.title: Orphan lane: show STATE + collapse terminal orphans (97 noisy, can't tell what's done)

phases.title: Orphan lane: show STATE + collapse terminal orphans (97 noisy, can't tell what's done)
phases.desired_end_state: Lane shows ALL unregistered tasks (terminal + active) with no phase, so 97 items look actionable when most are done. Fix: derive each orphan's phase, badge it (building/in-review/shipped/abandoned), and collapse/hide terminal ones so only actionable orphans show. Pairs with the Phase 2 derive-relocation. Auto-registration + register/dismiss buttons = Phase 3.

draft.end_state: When this phase is done, the orphan lane no longer shows 97 undifferentiated items that all look actionable. Every unregistered task with no phase carries a derived phase and a status badge — building, in-review, shipped, or abandoned — and the ones that are already finished (shipped or abandoned) are collapsed or hidden by default. The operator opens the lane and sees only the orphans that still need attention, with the done ones tucked away but reachable.
draft.why_now: The lane currently surfaces all unregistered, phase-less tasks together, so 97 items appear to demand action when most are already terminal. There is no way to tell what is done from what is live, which makes the lane untrustworthy and hides the small number of orphans that actually need a decision. This phase exists to restore signal by separating finished work from actionable work.
draft.scope: IN: deriving a phase for each orphan; assigning a status badge (building, in-review, shipped, abandoned); collapsing or hiding terminal orphans so only actionable ones show by default. OUT: automatic registration of orphans, and the register/dismiss buttons — both are explicitly deferred to a later phase (Phase 3). This phase changes how orphans are displayed and classified, not how they are acted upon or onboarded.
draft.constraints_reuse: Reuse the existing phase-derivation work rather than building classification from scratch — this phase pairs with the Phase 2 derive-relocation effort and should lean on the same derivation logic so the two stay consistent. The orphan lane itself and its current task listing must keep working; the change is additive (state + collapse), so tasks that are genuinely active must still appear and not be accidentally swept into the terminal/hidden bucket. Treat this as assembly on top of existing derivation, not a greenfield classifier.
draft.options_decision: The main fork is how terminal orphans are handled in the UI: (a) fully hide shipped/abandoned orphans by default with a way to reveal them, which gives the cleanest lane but risks the operator forgetting work exists; or (b) collapse them into a counted, expandable group that stays visible but out of the way, which keeps everything discoverable at the cost of a little more visual weight. A second, smaller fork is whether terminal means only shipped + abandoned, or whether in-review also counts as 'not actionable right now.' Recommendation: collapse terminal orphans into an expandable group (b) and treat only shipped + abandoned as terminal, keeping building and in-review visible — this reduces noise without making finished work invisible, and it is reversible if the operator wants stricter hiding later.
draft.risks_guardrails: Risk: an active orphan is misderived as terminal and disappears from view. Guardrail: default to showing, not hiding — only collapse on a confident shipped/abandoned signal, and make the collapsed group easy to expand. Risk: the derived phase or badge is wrong and the operator mistrusts the lane again. Guardrail: keep the badge visible and the underlying task reachable so a wrong call is obvious and correctable. Risk: scope creep into registration/dismiss, which belongs to Phase 3. Guardrail: this phase only displays and classifies — it adds no action buttons and no auto-registration. Risk: divergence from the Phase 2 derivation. Guardrail: share the same derivation source so badges and relocation agree.
draft.done_gate: Done means: every orphan in the lane shows a derived phase and one of the four status badges; shipped and abandoned orphans are collapsed/hidden by default while building and in-review orphans remain visible; and the operator can expand to see the terminal ones. Checkable: the default lane view shows far fewer than 97 items (only the actionable ones), the collapsed group reports an accurate terminal count, and no genuinely active task is hidden. Tests should confirm badge assignment matches the derived phase, terminal orphans collapse, active orphans stay visible, and expanding reveals the hidden set.
draft.breakdown: 1) Derive a phase for each orphan, reusing the Phase 2 derivation logic. 2) Map each derived phase to a status badge (building, in-review, shipped, abandoned) and render it on every orphan. 3) Classify which badges count as terminal (proposed: shipped + abandoned). 4) Collapse or hide terminal orphans by default into an expandable, counted group, leaving actionable orphans in the main view. 5) Verify the default view shows only actionable orphans and that active tasks are never swept into the terminal bucket. 6) Add tests covering badge assignment, collapse behavior, and the visible/hidden split.

decisions: Collapse terminal orphans into a visible, expandable group, or hide them fully by default?
Does 'terminal' mean only shipped + abandoned, or should in-review also be treated as not-actionable?
How confident must the derived signal be before an orphan is auto-collapsed as done?

handoff.directive: Work with Larry to finalize this brainstorm and author the spec at agents/beacon/specs/orphan-lane-show-state-collapse-terminal-orphans.md in ourliberty-agent-core; he will mark it Ready to spec.

phases.title: System self-awareness - the standing brain
phases.desired_end_state: Move insight, status, and direction off Larry's laptop so the droplet team self-directs. Multi-phase; first slice = work-in-flight Narrator -> State Log.

closeout.summary: The system now keeps a living, plain-English picture of all work currently in progress, updated automatically and readable on demand — so you can ask "where are we on work in flight?" and get an answer without firing up a Claude session on your laptop. This is the first slice of a larger effort to move status, insight, and direction off your laptop and onto the always-on droplet team; the next phase can build the diagnosing and planning organs on top of this standing picture.
closeout.shipped: A continuously-updated work-in-flight log that tracks active projects, their progress, what's stuck, and what's in review, written automatically on a schedule in your terms. You can read it three ways — on the dashboard, by asking Beacon for "work in flight" or "state of work," or via a /state shortcut — and it honestly tells you when it's stale rather than guessing (PR #602).
closeout.changed_vs_spec: The build matched the plan's first slice. The one notable judgment call: an existing "catch me up" shortcut already owned phrases like "where are we" and "status," so this new standing log was deliberately given distinct phrases to avoid stepping on it — the two now coexist, one giving the always-current picture and the other giving what's changed since you last checked.
closeout.learnings: The team built this almost entirely by reusing machinery that already existed rather than reinventing it, which kept it cheap to run and fast to ship. It was also built to never break the system or itself — every part fails quietly and degrades gracefully instead of taking anything down, a pattern worth carrying into the next phases.

closeout.summary: Larry can now ask the assistant "where are we on work in flight?" and get a current, plain-English answer — what's active, building, in review, stuck, or waiting on him — without having to summon Claude. It's reachable three ways: directly through the assistant via phrases like "work in flight" or "/state", and through a dashboard endpoint (PR #602).
closeout.changed_vs_spec: Built as planned, by reusing existing pieces rather than rebuilding them. One deliberate adjustment: because a recently-shipped "catch me up" feature already answers "where are we" and "status," this new standing picture uses distinct phrases to avoid stepping on it — the two are complementary, one a live catch-up, the other an always-current snapshot.
closeout.learnings: Two assistant features can sound like they do the same thing while serving different needs (a fresh catch-up versus a standing picture); keeping their trigger phrases separate avoids confusion. The whole thing was designed to stay cheap and fail gracefully — if any part can't be read, it reports what it can rather than going dark.

phases.title: System self-awareness - Slice 1b (Where are we)
phases.desired_end_state: Read-only dashboard view of the live State Log (GET /api/system/state-log) — the glance surface for Slice 1. Build STRICTLY from the spec doc.

draft.end_state: When this phase is done, there is a new read-only dashboard page called "Where are we" that renders the live State Log at a glance. Larry can open the dashboard and immediately see the whole-system status — a plain-language headline of where things stand, plus panels for work in flight, active missions, and what's waiting on him — without having to ask the assistant or read the raw endpoint. The page only displays; it never takes actions or writes anything. It pulls its data through the same-origin proxy, handles loading, stale, error, and empty states gracefully, and visually matches the existing system pages.
draft.why_now: The previous slice already made the system narrate its own work-in-flight and shipped the live data endpoint, but right now Larry can only consume that narration by asking the assistant or hitting the raw endpoint. His preferred way to consume status is the dashboard — glance first, then skim, then drill in. This phase delivers that human surface so the work already done becomes something he can actually see at a glance.
draft.scope: IN: a single new read-only page that renders the live State Log — a top-of-page narrative headline with a freshness indicator, and skim-level panels for work in flight (building, in review, recently merged, and anything stuck called out prominently), active missions, and a 'waiting on you' teaser. Also in: a navigation entry that routes to the page, the types describing the endpoint's response, graceful loading/stale/error/empty handling, and a test suite. OUT: any write or action controls (this is read-only only); click-through 'full story' drill-down into a mission or PR; and the system-health synthesis, which is a later slice and stays held. This page is also explicitly separate from the existing missions/projects board — it does not touch that board's pipeline.
draft.constraints_reuse: This is assembly, not greenfield. Reuse the existing read-only system page as the template for layout, fetching, loading, error/stale handling, and the panel structure — mirror its patterns rather than inventing new ones. Fetch through the canonical same-origin proxy hook with a periodic refresh, and reuse the shared building-block components for error boundaries, the stale-data banner, the last-refresh and relative-time displays, and the loading state. Match the existing styling conventions and the navigation pattern. Authentication is inherited automatically from existing middleware, so no per-page gate code. Two things must not break: the page must never call the backend host directly — always through the same-origin proxy — and it must not touch the existing missions/projects board, which is a deliberately distinct surface.
draft.options_decision: The spec is prescriptive, so most choices are already settled, but a couple of real forks remain. First, how defensively to type the endpoint's response: the snapshot may carry minor additions and one field is currently reserved/empty, so the fork is type-it-loosely-now (optional fields, fewer breakages as the backend evolves, but weaker compile-time guarantees) versus type-it-strictly against today's exact shape (stronger guarantees, but more churn when the backend adds fields). Recommendation: type defensively with optional fields where the shape is uncertain, and verify field shapes against the live endpoint while building. Second, where to place the new entry in the navigation: among the diagnostic/system entries near the existing live-system view. Recommendation: place it in that diagnostic cluster so it sits alongside related system views.
draft.risks_guardrails: Risk: the page accidentally calls the backend host directly instead of the same-origin proxy — guardrail: route every fetch through the canonical proxy hook and add a test that asserts the proxy path is used and the direct host is not. Risk: the live response shape drifts from what the page expects and a panel crashes — guardrail: type defensively with optional fields, verify against the live endpoint while building, and wrap each panel in an error boundary so one panel failing can't take down the page. Risk: the data is stale or the fetch fails and Larry trusts an out-of-date view — guardrail: show a stale banner on the stale flag or on fetch error, and surface a freshness timestamp. Risk: an empty or not-yet-written state renders as a confusing blank or crash — guardrail: explicit loading and friendly empty states. Risk: scope creep into drill-downs, health synthesis, or any action controls — guardrail: hold the line on read-only and the named out-of-scope items.
draft.done_gate: It's done when: the new page renders the live narrative plus the structured-snapshot panels, read-only; loading, error/stale, and empty states are all handled without crashing and panel render errors are contained by the per-panel error boundaries; the page fetches only via the same-origin proxy and never the backend host directly; the navigation entry is present and routes correctly with inherited auth; and the new test suite passes. Tests should mirror the existing comparable page's test approach: assert the header and narrative render on success, assert the fetch goes to the proxy path and not the direct host, assert the stale banner shows on a fetch error, and assert the snapshot panels (work-in-flight, missions, waiting-on-you) render. The finished page should also visually match the existing system page it mirrors.
draft.breakdown: Proposed steps: (1) Add the response types for the endpoint, including the nested snapshot and provenance shapes, typed defensively and verified against the live endpoint while building. (2) Build the page itself in the glance-then-skim layout: the narrative headline with freshness line and stale banner at top, then the skim panels — work in flight (with stuck items called out prominently), active missions, waiting-on-you highlighted, and a placeholder for the reserved health field — plus loading and empty states. (3) Add the navigation entry routing to the new page in the diagnostic cluster. (4) Write the test suite mirroring the existing comparable page's tests, covering success rendering, proxy-only fetching, stale-on-error, and panel rendering. These steps are mostly sequential (types underpin the page; the page underpins its tests), with the navigation entry independent and parallelizable.

decisions: Confirm read-only-only is the right call for this phase — no action or write controls of any kind, even small ones.
Confirm the reserved health field stays out of scope this slice (shown as a 'coming soon' placeholder) rather than being pulled forward.
Confirm where the navigation entry should sit — in the diagnostic cluster near the existing live-system view, or somewhere more prominent.
Confirm the data freshness expectation is acceptable — the underlying log refreshes roughly every ten minutes and the page polls every thirty seconds on top of that.

closeout.summary: The new "Where are we" dashboard page shipped (PR #73): Larry can now open the dashboard and see whole-system status at a glance instead of having to ask Beacon. closeout.shipped: A read-only "Where are we" page that shows the live system status in plain language — a headline summary plus skim panels for work in flight (including a prominent callout when something is stuck), active missions, and what's waiting on you. It's reachable from the dashboard's navigation and shows nothing but status — no buttons or actions.

closeout.learnings: The field shapes were verified against the live system data while building rather than assumed, and the data is pulled only through the safe same-origin path (never the server directly) — both confirmed by tests. One open item: a reviewer still needs to confirm the page renders correctly against the live deployed system.

phases.title: System self-awareness - Slice 2a (Waiting on Larry)
phases.desired_end_state: Extend the State Log's waiting_on_larry into an itemized cross-source list (parked + pending approvals + for-Larry escalations), read-only, reusing existing sources. Build STRICTLY from the spec doc.

draft.end_state: When this phase is done, the State Log no longer shows a single vague 'waiting on Larry' signal. Instead it shows an itemized, read-only list that pulls together everything currently blocked on the operator from across the existing sources: items that have been parked, approvals that are pending, and escalations explicitly raised for the operator. Each entry names what it is and where it came from, so the operator can see his full queue of blocking decisions in one place at a glance.
draft.why_now: Slice 1 established the State Log and its high-level 'waiting on Larry' indicator. That indicator tells the operator that something is waiting but not what or how much, which means he still has to go hunting across separate places to act on it. This slice is the natural next step: turn that single flag into an itemized list so the signal becomes actionable. The exact trigger and any deadline are not stated in the facts and should be confirmed.
draft.scope: IN: extending the existing State Log 'waiting on Larry' element into an itemized list; aggregating three existing sources of blocked items — parked items, pending approvals, and for-Larry escalations — into one read-only view; building strictly to what the spec document specifies. OUT: writing back to or mutating any of the underlying sources (this is read-only); adding new sources of blocking items beyond the three named; changing how items get parked, approved, or escalated in the first place. Anything not covered by the spec doc is out of scope until the spec says otherwise.
draft.constraints_reuse: This is assembly, not greenfield. Reuse the existing State Log surface from Slice 1 and the existing data sources for parked items, pending approvals, and for-Larry escalations rather than creating new stores or new ways of tracking blocked work. The read-only contract must not break: producing this list must not alter, resolve, re-order, or otherwise side-effect the underlying items. The existing Slice 1 'waiting on Larry' behavior and the rest of the State Log must continue to work unchanged. The exact source locations and their read interfaces are defined in the spec doc and should be taken from there.
draft.options_decision: The main fork is how the three sources are combined. Option A: aggregate them live at read time each time the State Log is viewed — always current, no staleness, but cost and latency depend on how expensive the three reads are. Option B: aggregate into a cached/materialized list refreshed on a cycle — cheaper and faster to render, but can show a slightly stale picture of what is waiting. A second fork is presentation: one flat merged list versus grouping by source (parked / pending approvals / escalations). The spec doc may already settle these; where it does, follow it. Recommendation pending the spec — provisionally, live aggregation with source-grouped display, since a decisions queue is most useful when it is accurate and its origins are visible. Confirm against the spec before locking.
draft.risks_guardrails: Risk: the read-only intent is violated and aggregating accidentally mutates or resolves an underlying item — guardrail: treat all three sources as strictly read-only and verify no write paths are touched. Risk: duplicate or double-counted entries when the same blocking item appears in more than one source — guardrail: define a de-duplication / identity rule in the spec so each real item shows once. Risk: drift from Slice 1 so the itemized count disagrees with the existing top-level 'waiting on Larry' flag — guardrail: make the flag and the list derive from the same aggregation. Risk: a slow or unavailable source degrades the whole State Log — guardrail: isolate per-source failures so one bad source does not blank the view. Risk: scope creep beyond the spec — guardrail: build strictly from the spec doc and defer anything not in it.
draft.done_gate: Done when: the State Log renders an itemized list of everything waiting on the operator, drawn from all three existing sources; each entry is identifiable and attributed to its source; the view is verifiably read-only (the underlying parked items, pending approvals, and escalations are unchanged after viewing); the itemized total is consistent with the existing Slice 1 'waiting on Larry' indicator; and the build matches the spec doc. Tests: parked items, pending approvals, and escalations each appear in the list; an empty source and an all-empty state render cleanly; duplicates across sources collapse per the spec's identity rule; a viewing pass leaves every source byte-for-byte unchanged; one unavailable source does not break the other two or the rest of the State Log.
draft.breakdown: Step 1: read the spec doc and pin down the exact three source interfaces, the entry shape, the de-duplication rule, and the display format it prescribes. Step 2: build a read-only aggregator that reads parked items, pending approvals, and for-Larry escalations and normalizes them into a common entry shape. Step 3: apply the de-duplication / identity rule so each real blocking item appears once. Step 4: wire the aggregated list into the existing State Log surface and reconcile it with the Slice 1 'waiting on Larry' indicator so they agree. Step 5: handle per-source failure isolation so one bad source degrades gracefully. Step 6: tests covering presence of each source, empty/all-empty states, de-duplication, the read-only guarantee, and source-failure isolation. Sequence may shift once the spec is read.

decisions: Live aggregation at view time vs. a cached list refreshed on a cycle — accuracy vs. cost/latency.
Display as one flat merged list or grouped by source (parked / approvals / escalations).
When the same item shows up in two sources, how to decide it is 'the same' and which source wins.
How a slow or unavailable source should behave — hide that section, show a placeholder, or surface an error.

phases.title: System self-awareness - Slice 2b (Waiting-on-Larry render)
phases.desired_end_state: Render the itemized waiting_on_larry.items[] on the /where-we-are 'Waiting on you' panel: source badge + title + plain-English why + relative age, in the substrate's order. Link approvals/escalations to /approvals, parked to /missions; reuse the Slice-1b page + Approvals tab, do not rebuild. Normalize the parked why dict-repr via cleanWhy. Update lib/types + extend vitest. Full spec: agents/beacon/specs/system-awareness-slice-2b-waiting-on-larry-render.md

draft.end_state: When this phase is done, the 'Waiting on you' panel on the where-we-are page no longer shows just a bare count of parked items. It shows the actual list: every thing waiting on Larry rendered as its own row with a small source label (escalation, approval, or parked), a plain-English title, a one-line reason, and how long it's been waiting — kept in the order the system already decided is most urgent. Each row links straight to where Larry acts on it: approvals and escalations go to the Approvals view, parked items go to the Missions funnel. The page opens and answers, in plain language, both 'where does everything stand' and 'what needs me,' one click from acting.
draft.why_now: The earlier slices built up to exactly this. One slice gave Larry the whole-system glance; the most recent one taught the underlying system to produce the itemized 'what needs you' data — a per-source, ordered, bounded list. But the page still only renders a number, so Larry can see that, say, twenty-two things are waiting on him but not what they are or where to go. This panel is the payoff of the entire 'what needs Larry' arc; rendering the list is the last piece that makes the whole effort usable.
draft.scope: IN: rendering the itemized waiting list on the existing 'Waiting on you' panel — source label, title, plain-English reason, relative age, in the order the system already provides; linking approval/escalation rows to the Approvals view and parked rows to the Missions funnel; normalizing the messy machine-formatted reason text on parked items into plain English; a kept summary count, a calm empty state, and a 'more waiting' note when the list is capped; updating the data type definition to match the real shape and extending the existing tests. OUT: rebuilding or changing the Approvals view or the Missions funnel (link out only, no actions or writes in this panel); per-item detail or drill-down panes; any health summary; and the separate upstream cleanup that would make the reason text clean at the source.
draft.constraints_reuse: This is assembly, not greenfield. Extend the existing where-we-are page and the single panel function inside it — keep the page structure, the shared panel wrapper, the loading and stale and empty handling, and every other panel untouched. The data is already fetched by the page's existing poll, so no new data fetching is added; this is rendering plus types only. Reuse the existing shared components and styling tokens already used across these pages, and the existing automatic auth. The hard boundary: the Approvals view and the Missions funnel are the homes for those items — this panel links to them and must not re-implement their lists, queries, or actions. Existing tests must stay green, and the panel must keep behaving like the rest of the page on loading, stale, empty, and error states without crashing.
draft.options_decision: Fork one — what to do about the parked items' reason text, which today arrives as a messy machine-formatted blob rather than a sentence. Option A: render a small, tested cleanup helper in this panel that pulls out the human summary, falling back to showing nothing rather than the raw blob. Option B: wait for the separate upstream fix that would make the system emit clean text at the source. Trade-off: A ships now and is defensive even after the upstream fix lands (it just becomes a pass-through), but is belt-and-suspenders work; B is cleaner long-term but blocks this visible payoff on unrelated work. Recommendation: A — defend in the panel now, let the upstream cleanup proceed as its own follow-up. Fork two — how loud to make a critical escalation. Option A: every source gets the same calm treatment, distinguished only by a neutral label color. Option B: a critical-severity escalation gets a stronger visual cue. Trade-off: louder is more useful in a real incident but risks the panel feeling alarmist when, today, the list is entirely low-urgency parked items. Recommendation: keep it calm by default with at most a subtle bump for critical, since today nothing critical is even flowing.
draft.risks_guardrails: Risk: the panel shows the raw machine-formatted reason blob to Larry, violating plain-language-first. Guardrail: a pure, tested cleanup helper that extracts the human summary and renders nothing rather than the blob if it can't, with the test cases as the contract. Risk: accidentally re-sorting the list and undoing the urgency ordering the system already applied. Guardrail: render strictly in the order received, asserted in tests. Risk: drifting into rebuilding the Approvals view or adding actions here. Guardrail: this panel is read-only and links out only — no write or action controls, enforced by the scope boundary and review. Risk: an older or partial data snapshot crashes the panel or shows a broken empty list. Guardrail: keep the prior count-only behavior as a fallback when the itemized list is absent, with a back-compat test. Risk: today only one of the three source types actually has data, so the other two paths go untested in production. Guardrail: tests cover all three source types with representative items even though two are empty live today.
draft.done_gate: It's done when the panel renders the itemized list — source label, title, plain-English reason, relative age — in the system's order; when no parked item ever shows the raw machine-formatted reason blob; when approval and escalation rows link to the Approvals view and parked rows link to the Missions funnel, with the Approvals view left unrebuilt; when a summary count is kept and the empty, loading, and stale states behave like the rest of the page without crashing; and when the data type matches the real shape. Tests prove it: the list renders each item's title and source label, the messy parked reason is shown normalized with no raw blob, the links resolve to the right destinations, the summary count reflects the true total, the capped-list note appears when the list is truncated, the empty state shows when nothing is waiting, and the legacy count-only shape still renders. The existing test suite stays green.
draft.breakdown: Step one: tighten the data type definition for the waiting-on-you shape to match what the system actually emits — the item fields, the source and severity values, the counts, and the truncation flag — so typos are caught and older snapshots still type-check. Step two: extend the single panel to render the summary count, then the itemized rows (label, title, cleaned reason, relative age, action link) in the given order, plus the capped-list note, the calm empty state, and the back-compat fallback to the old count box. Step three: add the small pure helpers the panel needs — relative-age formatting, the reason-text cleanup, and the source-to-destination link mapping — kept module-scoped and individually tested. Step four: extend the existing test suite with representative items across all three sources (including a parked item whose reason is the messy blob) and assertions for titles, labels, normalized reason, resolved links, summary count, the capped note, the empty state, and back-compat, plus focused unit tests on the helpers. These map cleanly onto the four deliverables already laid out in the full spec.

decisions: Ship the in-panel reason cleanup now and treat the upstream source fix as a separate follow-up, rather than waiting for the source to emit clean text — confirm that's the call.
How loud should a critical escalation look: same calm styling as everything else, or a stronger visual cue when severity is critical?
Is capping the visible list with a 'more waiting' note (rather than showing all of them) the right behavior, or do you want a way to expand the full list?

projects.title: Auto-retire Done pipeline cards (follow-up to phase-aware Complete & retire, merged #629/#77). A Done project should auto-retire after a visibility window (default ~48h since it reached Done) so the board self-cleans and Larry never has to click Complete & retire. Design: a healer tick (heal_projects_store or a new heal_pipeline_retire) scans ACTIVE projects with rollup status 'done', computes done-at = max(phase.updated_at where lifecycle_state=='done'), and when now-done_at > window flips state active->retired (single-committer: healer owns projects.json). The 'retired' state + suppresses_funnel_source() already exist (active+retired keep the funnel source suppressed; only archived returns it). Card stays visible as a 'Done' win for the window, then clears. Window via config/env. Reversibility note: retired is terminal + suppressed, so add a 'recently retired' surface later if needed.

closeout.shipped: A timer was added so a finished project stays on the 'Actively working' board for roughly two days after it's done, then quietly retires on its own (PR #667). The wait time is adjustable via a setting if 48 hours ever feels wrong.
closeout.changed_vs_spec: It came in exactly as planned — no new machinery, just one waiting period added to the auto-retire that was already running. Nothing diverged from the design.
closeout.learnings: Auto-retire was already live but fired the instant a project finished, which is why the Done win vanished before you ever saw it — the real fix was 'make it wait,' not 'make it retire.' By design it errs toward keeping a card on the board if its finish time is unclear, so nothing disappears prematurely; the manual button stays as a backstop.

projects.title: Mirror review visibility for session-less PRs

phases.title: Mirror review visibility for session-less PRs
phases.desired_end_state: Close the session-less-PR review gaps #653/#645 exposed: (A) Mirror posts its findings as an idempotent PR comment on every non-PASS so they're never invisible; (B) classify the no-session outcome by marker_type (self-healing / action-needed / decision-needed); (C) route human-needed buckets to Larry's surfaces (decision->Approvals tab, action->larry_alert/Operator Action Queue) — never a PR comment he won't read; (E) heal_pipeline_stall backstop for silent red-status PRs. Spec dispatched (spec-mirror-review-visibility-001); 3-step build held until orchestrator-terminal-signal-hardening lands (shared files).

draft.end_state: When this phase is done, no Mirror review of a session-less PR can quietly disappear. Any review that isn't a clean pass leaves a visible, de-duplicated note on the PR itself. Every no-session outcome is sorted into one of three buckets — it heals itself, it needs someone to act, or it needs someone to decide — and the ones that need a human reach Larry where he actually looks: decisions show up in his approvals surface, actions land in his alert and operator action queue, and the self-healing ones quietly resolve without pinging him. On top of that, a PR that goes silently red is caught by a backstop instead of sitting unnoticed.
draft.why_now: Two recent session-less PRs slipped through and made the gap concrete: when a PR has no active session, Mirror's findings had nowhere to go. There was no guaranteed comment and no routing, so real problems sat invisible until someone happened to notice. The review path works fine for session-based PRs, so this is specifically about closing the no-session case before more reviews go unseen.
draft.scope: IN: posting an idempotent PR comment on every non-PASS session-less review; classifying the no-session outcome into self-healing, action-needed, and decision-needed; routing the human-needed buckets to the right operator surfaces (decisions to the approvals view, actions to the alert/operator action queue) rather than a PR comment Larry won't read; and a backstop that catches silently red PRs. OUT: changing what Mirror reviews or its pass/fail criteria; the session-based PR flow, which already surfaces correctly; and redesigning the approvals view or operator action queue themselves — we route into them as they exist.
draft.constraints_reuse: This is assembly, not greenfield. Reuse the existing marker-type classification rather than inventing a new taxonomy, the existing operator surfaces (approvals view, alert channel, operator action queue) as routing targets, and the existing healing/backstop machinery for the silent-red case. The session-based review path must keep working untouched. PR comments must be idempotent so re-runs update rather than pile up duplicates. One hard constraint: the build touches files that a separate in-flight hardening effort is also changing, so the work has to slot in after that lands to avoid conflicts.
draft.options_decision: There are a few real forks. First, how to make the PR comment idempotent: tag-and-update an existing comment, key off a stable marker, or look up by author/heading — find-and-update via a hidden marker is simplest and avoids spam. Second, how much to trust marker_type for classification: take it as authoritative, or apply our own mapping on top — trusting it is less code but exposes us to bad/missing markers. Third, what to do when an outcome is ambiguous or unclassifiable: default it to the human-visible decision path (safer, slightly noisier) or to the action path. Recommendation: update-by-marker for comments, trust marker_type but treat anything missing/unknown as a decision-needed item so it surfaces to a human rather than vanishing.
draft.risks_guardrails: Comment spam from re-running a review — guardrail: idempotency keyed on a stable marker so a repeat run edits the existing comment. Misclassification sending a needs-decision item to a silent channel — guardrail: default ambiguous or unknown markers to the human-visible decision path. Backstop firing on PRs that are legitimately and visibly red — guardrail: scope it to genuinely silent/stale red status, not every failure. File conflicts with the concurrent hardening effort — guardrail: hold the build until that work lands. Double-surfacing, where the same issue both posts a comment and pings an operator queue — guardrail: decide one clear rule for when both happen versus only the routed surface.
draft.done_gate: It's done when: a non-PASS session-less review produces exactly one PR comment, and re-running the review updates that comment instead of adding another; each no-session outcome is classified into self-healing, action-needed, or decision-needed; a decision-needed item appears in the approvals surface, an action-needed item appears in the alert/operator action queue, and a self-healing item produces no human ping; and a PR left silently red triggers the backstop. Tests cover each path: idempotent comment on repeat runs, correct bucket per marker type, correct routing target per bucket, and backstop firing on a silent red PR.
draft.breakdown: Three build steps, held until the shared-file hardening work lands. Step one: post an idempotent PR comment on every non-PASS session-less review. Step two: classify the no-session outcome by marker type into self-healing, action-needed, and decision-needed. Step three: route the human-needed buckets to their operator surfaces (decisions to approvals, actions to the alert/operator queue) and add the silent-red backstop. The spec is already written; the ordering dependency on the hardening effort is itself a tracked precondition rather than a build step.

decisions: When an outcome can't be cleanly classified, should it default to the human-visible decision path (safer but noisier) or the action path?
Should every non-PASS leave a PR comment even when the item is also routed to an operator surface, or only when it isn't routed elsewhere, to avoid double-surfacing?
How aggressive should the silent-red backstop be — err toward catching more (more false positives) or fewer (risk of misses)?
Confirm building after the shared-file hardening effort lands, versus splitting the work to start the independent pieces now.

phases.title: Missions Phase 4b.2 — closed-card doorbell
phases.desired_end_state: The closed-card unread badge deferred from Phase 4b (PR #662). Server-side fix: project a compact doorbell signal (newest team_to_larry message id/ts + blocked flag) onto the card-list payload the kanban already polls (Contract E, agent-core), then render the closed-card badge from it (Contract F, dashboard). Rides the existing poll — no new endpoint, no background thread-polling (respects Phase 4b Contract A). Spec dispatched (spec-phase4b2-closed-card-doorbell-001); 2-step build follows after the spec merges.

draft.end_state: When this phase is done, a card that has been closed still tells the operator at a glance whether it has unread messages waiting from the team — the closed card shows an unread badge, the same way open cards already do. The signal comes from the server: the card-list data the board already fetches will carry a small marker for each card (the most recent team-to-operator message, with its timestamp, plus a flag for whether the card is blocked), and the board paints the closed-card badge directly from that marker. Nothing new is polled and no new endpoint exists; the badge simply rides along on the data already moving.
draft.why_now: This is the piece that was intentionally cut from the previous phase to keep that phase shippable — it was deferred rather than dropped, so it is now the named follow-up. The previous phase deliberately ruled out adding background polling to make this work, which left closed cards unable to show unread state. Picking it up now closes that gap while the design decisions and surrounding code from the previous phase are still fresh and the agreed approach (piggyback on the existing poll) is already settled.
draft.scope: IN: adding a compact unread signal for each card onto the existing card-list payload on the server side (newest team-to-operator message id and timestamp, plus a blocked indicator); rendering an unread badge on closed cards from that signal in the board UI. OUT: any new endpoint; any new background or per-thread polling; changing how open-card badges already work; redesigning the message model or the board's existing fetch cadence. Anything beyond making closed cards reflect unread state through the data the board already receives is out.
draft.constraints_reuse: Reuse, don't rebuild: the board already polls a card-list payload on a set cadence — the unread signal is attached to that same payload, and the badge reuses the existing badge rendering rather than introducing a new component or fetch path. Two things must not break: the previous phase's commitment to no new background or thread-level polling must hold, and the open-card unread behavior that already works must remain unchanged. The change is additive — one new field flowing through an existing channel, read by existing UI.
draft.options_decision: The main fork is what to pack into the per-card signal. Option A: a minimal marker (newest team-to-operator message id, its timestamp, and a blocked flag) and let the UI decide read/unread by comparing against what the operator has already seen — smallest payload, keeps read-state logic where it already lives, but relies on the UI having a reliable notion of last-seen. Option B: have the server compute and send an explicit unread boolean per card — simplest for the UI, but pushes read-state knowledge to the server and risks drifting from how open cards already determine unread. A secondary fork is how the badge looks on a closed card: identical to the open-card badge, or visually distinct to signal the card is closed-but-waiting. Recommendation: Option A with a badge that matches the existing open-card style, because it stays closest to current behavior and adds the least new surface — escalate to a distinct style only if closed-but-unread proves easy to overlook.
draft.risks_guardrails: Risk: the signal silently inflates the card-list payload or its compute cost as card counts grow — guardrail: keep the per-card field to the few primitive values named and confirm payload size and response time stay in line with today's. Risk: closed-card and open-card badges disagree about what counts as unread, confusing the operator — guardrail: derive both from the same read/unread logic rather than a parallel path. Risk: scope creep back toward background polling to make the badge 'live' — guardrail: hold the line that the badge only updates on the existing poll, exactly as agreed in the prior phase. Risk: a card with no team-to-operator messages or an unusual state renders a stray or missing badge — guardrail: define and test the empty/blocked cases explicitly.
draft.done_gate: Done means: a closed card with unread team-to-operator messages visibly shows an unread badge; a closed card with nothing unread shows none; the badge state matches what the equivalent open card would show; and no new endpoint or background/thread polling was introduced — the badge updates only when the existing card-list poll refreshes. Tests should cover the server attaching the correct per-card signal (including the no-messages and blocked cases), the UI rendering the badge from that signal, and a check that open-card unread behavior is unchanged.
draft.breakdown: Step one (server): add the compact per-card unread signal to the existing card-list payload — the newest team-to-operator message id and timestamp plus the blocked flag — without adding any endpoint or new polling, and with tests for the populated, empty, and blocked cases. Step two (UI): render the closed-card unread badge from that signal, reusing the existing badge, and confirm it updates on the normal poll and that open-card behavior is untouched. The detailed design lands first as a spec; the two build steps follow once that spec is agreed.

decisions: Should the server send a minimal marker and let the UI decide unread, or send an explicit unread flag per card?
Should the closed-card badge look identical to the open-card badge, or be visually distinct to signal 'closed but waiting'?
Is it acceptable that the badge only refreshes on the existing poll (not live), per the no-new-polling rule?

phases.desired_end_state: Make the build-sequence advancer + stall backstops propagate terminal agent outcomes correctly. Root cause: chain_event_says_failed queries event types the shipper never emits (forge_reject/mirror_* vs the real preflight_reject/review_escalate), so only the merge path is wired and non-merge terminals false-strand to the 4h timer with a misattributed reason. Re-scoped to 2 steps after reconciling vs #665/#668 (which already shipped the no-session mechanical recovery + most backstop fixes): Step 1 advancer event-type realign + stall attribution; Step 2 push-signal non-merge terminals + pr_url/substatus at PR-open.

phases.title: Operator Needs-You Feed
phases.desired_end_state: Complete the /where-we-are Waiting-on-You board + doorbell: feed the two missing needs-you classes (critical alerts the healers couldn't auto-fix; CLARIFY-exhausted builds) through the existing promote_alerts gate as durable, self-clearing for-Larry records; itemize paused / stuck-dispatched build sequences; and add live Resume/Skip/Cancel steering buttons via a new audited POST endpoint. Supersedes the archived e4-4g operator-action-queue.

closeout.summary: The "Waiting on You" board and doorbell alert are now the complete, single place to see everything that needs your attention — including the two kinds of items that used to only flash by in Telegram, plus paused or stuck work, each with Resume/Skip/Cancel buttons you can press right there. The next phase can build on a finished front door: anything that genuinely needs you now lands in one spot and clears itself once handled.
closeout.shipped: Two previously-buried classes now appear on the board: urgent problems the system couldn't fix on its own, and builds that got stuck after asking you all the questions they were allowed to. Paused and stalled work is itemized with live Resume/Skip/Cancel buttons (with a confirm step before anything destructive), delivered across PRs #685, #706, and #93.
closeout.changed_vs_spec: The build largely followed the plan. The one notable choice was reusing the existing attention-routing machinery and battle-tested action buttons rather than building new versions from scratch, which the original draft had leaned toward.
closeout.learnings: The key discovery was that the "does this need the CEO?" decision logic already existed and was already running — so the work became feeding the board from that one source instead of inventing a second one, which avoids double-pinging you. A reusable signal component was also created that future "needs-you" items can plug into without new plumbing.

phases.title: Forge WIP-only session-death auto-redispatch
phases.desired_end_state: New bounded, poll-based healer (scripts/heal_forge_wip_only_redispatch.py + systemd timer) that detects a Forge/Mirror dispatch whose session died leaving ONLY the [WIP][session-start] checkpoint commit (no build commit, no PR, inbox already archived) and mechanically re-queues the SAME task once with strict dedup, escalating to Larry only when auto-recovery is exhausted. Closes the coverage gap behind Pulse G-rule 'Forge-timeout-worktree-missing-retry-loop' (3 observed instances, latest 2026-06-24 reconcile-hardening-mission-shipped-001).
